source.supplement_to: Kaack, Fugate & Thomas 2024, All Earth, DOI 10.1080/27669645.2024.2419236

catalogue.selection_rule: all catalogue rows identifying ADV velocity components

published_physical_result.evidence_class: external published field evidence, not a Tampa result
published_physical_result.summary: The paired Estero Bay study reports lower near-bed velocity and generally lower near-bottom shear stress at the Thalassia vegetated site than at the nearby barren site under similar hydrologic forcing.
published_physical_result.role: Supports the physical plausibility of direct canopy-scale velocity measurement; does not validate the Tampa attenuation-to-future-persistence hypothesis.

raw_reanalysis.reason: PANGAEA binary delivery returned persistent HTTP 503 during the reproducible CI attempt.
raw_reanalysis.rule: Do not substitute plotted-value digitization or selectively transcribed values as if they were the raw benchmark.

novelty_boundary: Showing that seagrass canopies attenuate flow is not the novel Tampa claim.
The Tampa test is whether measured attenuation predicts a future quantitative trajectory in long-monitored meadows.
A secondary Tampa-specific question is whether alternative-seagrass occupancy provides hydrodynamic functional insurance when Thalassia declines.
